NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 21 : Major stock indexes climbed on Wednesday, lifted by more strong results from AI-focused companies, while France's 10-year bond yield hit 5 per cent for the first time since 2002 due to growing concern about the country's economic outlook. The Nasdaq gained more than 1 per cent, with Super Micro shares rising 9.5 per cent after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates.  Shares of SpaceX shot up 7.8 per cent after Elon Musk said late on Tuesday that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea." SpaceX also posted its first profit as a public company. AI-related shares sold off ahead of third-quarter results on investor worries about how long the AI trade can last.

"A lot of the concerns that we had over the last few weeks that sent the market lower are being alleviated," said Adam Sarhan, chief executive of 50 Park Investments in New York. Earnings "are coming in mixed to stronger than expected," which he called a relief. "Tech stocks fell hard last week on fears that the AI party is over," he said. In addition, US bond yields have been falling after their recent run higher, and US interest rate hike expectations have waned, he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 360.21 points, or 0.69 per cent, to close at 52,856.09, the S&P 500 rose 44.60 points, or 0.58 per cent, to 7,757.17 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 278.04 points, or 1.05 per cent, to 26,702.86. After the closing bell, Meta Platforms shares gained after the Facebook owner raised the lower end of its annual spending forecast. Meta ended the regular session up 0.5 per cent. Tesla shares also rose in after-hours trading as it reported a surprise positive cash flow for the third quarter. The stock ended the regular session up 3.4 per cent.  MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 7.48 points, or 0.7 per cent, to 1,137.88. The pan-European STOXX 600 index climbed 0.92 per cent. US Treasury yields edged lower, with the yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note shedding 0.6 basis point to 5.111 per cent.  Stocks have slipped of late and bonds have rallied due to concerns about the effect of higher borrowing costs on AI infrastructure stocks. FRENCH BOND YIELDS RISE French bond yields rose again, with 10-year bond yields hitting a new 24-year high above 5 per cent. The premium on French yields over benchmark 10-year German Bunds has also edged back toward early October's 15-year high of nearly 160 bps. French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence at protests planned in the coming days, and dismissed as "stupid" and "unacceptable" comments from some foreign leaders about the unrest.   French supermarket operator Carrefour fell about 13 per cent after it cut its guidance due to the recent protests. The euro was nearly flat at $1.1237. The US dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.14 per cent to 101.65.  The Australian dollar gained after Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser told a Citi conference that the inflation outlook looked "materially worse." The Aussie gained 0.41 per cent versus the greenback to $0.7031. Benchmark oil futures ended little changed, with investors weighing possible progress toward Russia-Ukraine talks against data showing a fall in US oil stocks. Brent crude rose 3 cents to settle at $108.82 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude fell 67 cents, or 0.7 per cent, to settle at $97.15.

Source: Reuters

Oct 21 : A Chinese-linked hacking group used an AI-driven penetration testing tool to compromise IT services firm ConnectWise as part of a campaign that targeted hundreds of organizations globally, Microsoft said on Wednesday. ConnectWise did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Microsoft's conclusions, although a statement posted to the company's website on October 16 said it was "investigating recent attempts of unauthorized access associated with the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment." The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing regularly denies conducting or condoning cyber-enabled data theft. The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, used an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign, Microsoft said.

There are multiple tools used to conduct penetration testing, a form of legitimate testing of the security of networks or services. ARTEX allows users to use any AI model to automate a variety of penetration testing tasks and can be configured to run autonomous tasks including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, Microsoft said.  The attack targeted organizations across a wide variety of sectors, including aerospace, defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, think tanks and nonprofits, Microsoft said. While the majority of the targeting was not successful, Microsoft said, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence — or high-level access that could continue even after cleanup efforts — at many organizations in a brief time.

Oct 21 : Walmart on Wednesday intrduced new tools that will allow artificial intelligence agents to shop and complete transactions for customers, as the retailer seeks to position itself in the growing use of AI-powered assistants in online commerce. The move underscores Walmart's push into AI-enabled shopping, and strikes a contrast with Amazon, which has sought to limit third-party AI shopping agents' access to its platform. Here are the details: • The retailer said it will roll out "Agent Profiles" next month, enabling shoppers to authorize individual AI agents, track their purchases separately and set spending limit or require approval for each transaction

FAST

Oct 21 : Crocodilians — today's crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials and their many extinct relatives — have been a roaring success since debuting more than 240 million years ago. And new research identifies one important factor in their success — stubbornly keeping to warm climates throughout their history. In fact, the researchers said, this trait may help explain why crocs as a group survived the asteroid strike 66 million years ago that doomed the dinosaurs, along with certain physiological characteristics that make them one tough bunch of reptiles. The crocodilian evolutionary lineage, called Pseudosuchia, arose during the Triassic Period in the aftermath of Earth's worst mass extinction event at the end of the Permian, appearing on the scene millions of years before the first dinosaurs and mammals. The researchers tracked the geographic range for crocs during their entire history, guided by an evolutionary tree of more than 400 extinct and living species. They used data from more than 7,000 fossils and geographic records of modern crocs such as the alligators of Florida, saltwater crocodiles of Australia, gharials of India, caimans of Brazil and more.

They combined this information with 52 global palaeoclimate reconstructions to determine the climatic conditions under which crocs lived over time. While other groups such as dinosaurs and mammals conquered a variety of climates, the study showed that crocs consistently kept to warm climes. "Rather than continually adapting to new climatic conditions, they largely tracked suitable environments as these shifted geographically, expanding towards the poles during warmer periods and retreating towards the equator during cooler ones," said University College London vertebrate paleontologist Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, lead author of the research published in the journal Science Advances. For example, during an exceptionally warm moment in Earth's history around 50 million years ago, Chiarenza said, crocs inhabited high-latitude regions of North America, Europe and even Antarctica. "One of the most striking patterns is the repeated expansion and contraction of suitable habitat in response to global temperature changes," Chiarenza said. While living crocs are primarily semiaquatic ambush predators, their extinct relatives included a broad diversity of forms, University College London paleontologist and study co-author Philip Mannion said. "They have occupied almost every conceivable ecological role," Chiarenza said. There were fully land-dwelling apex predators like 30-foot-long (9-meter-long) Fasolasuchus, pug-snouted herbivores like Simosuchus, armored plant-eaters like Aetosaurus, mollusk-eaters like Kuttanacaiman, filter-feeders like Mourasuchus and ocean-going types like Metriorhynchus. During the age of dinosaurs, there also were semiaquatic crocs like Deinosuchus up to 40 feet (12 meters) long that may have rivaled Tyrannosaurus in mass. "Modern crocodilians are only the surviving remnants of a once extraordinarily diverse evolutionary group," Chiarenza said. DISASTER FROM ABOVE The asteroid strike at a site called Chicxulub off the coast of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula at the end of the Cretaceous unleashed a global environmental cataclysm. Three-quarters of Earth's species including the dinosaurs, aside from their bird descendants, vanished. The crocs survived. "The Chicxulub impact caused a dramatic reduction in incoming sunlight, producing an impact winter and widespread environmental disruption. However, our climate simulations suggest that this cooling did not affect the availability of suitable climatic conditions equally for all groups," Chiarenza said. "Under all but the most extreme impact scenario we tested, tropical and subtropical regions retained climatic conditions suitable" for the crocs, Chiarenza said. This suggests that the longstanding association of crocs with warm and low-latitude environments may have placed some surviving populations in geographic refuges near the equator and in the subtropics where climatic conditions remained within their tolerances, Chiarenza said. For dinosaurs, there was a collapse of suitable habitat under these impact conditions. Crocs also possess physiological traits beneficial for times of environmental stress. They can enter states of dormancy to cope with harsh conditions — aestivation to survive extreme heat or drought, and brumation to withstand extreme cold. Crocs today, for instance, may dig burrows or encase themselves in hardened mud during severe droughts, slowing their heartbeat and breathing. "Following the Chicxulub impact, when sunlight was dramatically reduced and terrestrial primary productivity collapsed, the ability to reduce energy expenditure and survive periods of limited food availability could have been extremely advantageous," Chiarenza said. Crocs also are cold-blooded, while recent research points to at least some dinosaurs including Tyrannosaurus as warm-blooded. Baseline metabolic requirements for cold-blooded animals are much lower than for comparably sized warm-blooded animals. "That can become a significant advantage when food becomes scarce. Crocodilians can survive extended periods without feeding," Chiarenza said. "But even if an animal can survive prolonged starvation, it still needs environmental conditions that remain within its physiological limits."

Source: Reuters

Oct 21 : Europe's largest tech company SAP on Wednesday achieved a €10 billion ($11.2 billion) quarterly revenue milestone for the first time, while reporting a 26 per cent rise in current cloud backlog and lifting its 2026 revenue outlook to the upper end of its range. Cloud revenue rose 26 per cent to €6.67 billion in the third quarter while non-IFRS operating profit rose 18 per cent to €3.03 billion. SAP's cloud backlog at constant currencies grew 26 per cent to €24.14 billion ($27.11 billion), ahead of the 24 per cent to 25 per cent growth UBS had forecast. SAP held its operating profit outlook at €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion at constant currencies, a range trimmed in July for its recent acquisitions. SAP's order book is watched as a gauge of enterprise tech spending worldwide as its software suite runs accounting and payroll at many of the world's biggest companies. A miss on the measure in January sent the shares down 15 per cent in one day.  "AI was the main driver behind customers move to the cloud," in the quarter, CEO Christian Klein told analysts, with companies signing subscription contracts to get access to SAP's Joule assistant platform connecting to over 70 AI models. "SAP is not committing to a preferred model," he said.

Its profit margin widened to 29.5 per cent from 28.3 per cent while free cash flow rose 36 per cent to €1.72 billion. SAP now expects 2026 subscription revenue — access to software customers rent remotely rather than buy and run themselves — toward the top of its €25.8 billion to €26.2 billion forecast, up 23 per cent to 25 per cent. Including the declining classic licence business, it sees revenue of €36.3 billion to €36.8 billion, up 12 per cent to 13 per cent, at the top of its range.  Klein called it "an outstanding quarter." Customers are "investing in the technology behind" the company's AI strategy, he said. New cloud customers included AstraZeneca, Infineon. ($1 = 0.8903 euros)

Oct 21 : Meta introduced new non-voting shares on Wednesday to help fund the social media giant's costly AI expansion, as executives laid out their vision for organizing the company's future around its nascent AI agent business. Shares of the Facebook and Instagram parent rose more than 4 per cent in extended trading. Meta also forecast fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates and reported strong growth of its new consumer AI agent app Muse. The company has been pouring money into advanced chips and data centers to compete more aggressively with AI market leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, propelling it to the vanguard of an emerging consumer AI agent race while also eroding its historically strong free cash flow. Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively resulting in a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control.

Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up Muse accounts in a month and a half and growth remained strong. He said he expected Muse would eventually serve "billions of people" who would potentially generate more revenue than the average Meta user, forecasting the venture would give rise to the kind of network effect that helped build his social media empire. "Part of the reason why we're not just charging everyone up front to use this is we want to establish this Muse network, and we think that it's going to be more valuable for people at scale when there are a lot of people and businesses using Muse," Zuckerberg said on a conference call after Meta published its third-quarter financial report. HIGHER COSTS Still, Zuckerberg acknowledged that the costs of offering Muse were higher than those associated with many of Meta's other new products over the years, and said the company would move to monetize the agent "somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook." Meta CFO Susan Li forecast the company's AI businesses would begin contributing incremental revenue in 2027 and become "a meaningful source of revenue diversification over time." The executives also emphasized that AI would be the focus moving forward for Meta’s loss-making Reality Labs unit, which had led the charge on the company’s vision to build the “metaverse,” an immersive digital world that inspired its name change from Facebook to Meta in 2021. In their financial report, they said they “remain focused on improving Reality Labs profitability” and forecast its losses would narrow next year to around $15 billion “as we reallocate investment toward other priority areas, primarily AI.” The company raised the lower end of its annual spending forecast, now expecting capital expenditure to be between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from $130 billion to $145 billion expected previously. It reported a free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. Revenue for the third quarter came in better than expected at $64.60 billion, ahead of Wall Street estimates of $63.37 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Meta also projected fourth-quarter revenue between $73 billion and $76 billion, above estimates of $73.73 billion. The early popularity of Muse and the release of a competitive new series of AI models have helped Meta justify its spending to investors, even though some enterprises are restricting the agent's access over security concerns. "The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story," said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. LEGAL CHALLENGES Legal challenges are mounting, including a $25 billion penalty ordered by a judge in New Mexico earlier on Wednesday after a jury found Meta misled the state's residents about how it shared user data with third parties and enforced policies on hate speech and misinformation in a case related to British political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica. The $25 billion penalty is a "stark reminder of the current legal challenges Meta faces, which will continue into next year," Emarketer senior analyst Minda Smiley said. "Questions and concerns related to privacy and safety will only ramp up should AI agents become more mainstream, which could ultimately hurt Meta considering its reputation in this area." In August, Meta agreed to pay as much as $18 billion over a decade and restrict teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram to settle claims by nearly all US states alleging that Meta's platforms were designed to addict children. Meta posted diluted earnings per share of $3.83 in the quarter, a figure that would have been $7.40 had it not been for a $9.89 billion charge related to the August settlement. The agreement removed a significant regulatory hurdle that had weighed on Meta's stock and allowed the company to avoid a potentially lengthy trial that could have exposed more internal documents about its treatment of young users. Still, Meta warned in its guidance on Wednesday that it continued to face scrutiny and US trials around "youth-related issues" that could impact its financial results.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 21 : BlackRock rolled out another in a suite of exchange-traded funds tied to AI on Wednesday, even as the willingness of investors to wholeheartedly embrace the theme has hit speed bumps. The global asset manager said that its iShares Future Robotics and Related Technologies ETF will invest in companies that use intelligent machines to streamline repetitive tasks in industries such as transportation and manufacturing, which it said represents the next frontier in AI technologies. “Recent volatility is a reminder that AI is not a single trade and that investors need to be deliberate about where and how they take exposure," said Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock. That volatility does not change the firm's conviction on the AI theme, he added. "Expectations can shift quickly, adoption can develop unevenly and market risk remains concentrated in a relatively narrow group of companies," Jacobs said. Moreover, AI has emerged as a driver of both returns and risk even in broad market portfolios.

Oct 21 : Government websites across Europe went dark on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the most widely used programming languages on the web. The developers of PHP said on Wednesday they would release patches for two critical vulnerabilities, and EU cybersecurity officials warned organisations unable to apply the fixes to take affected websites offline. Here is what you need to know: WHAT IS PHP? PHP is a programming language that runs websites. It works behind the scenes. When a user loads a page, the server running PHP assembles the content and sends the finished page to the browser.

It is free, open source and maintained by volunteers. Site owners rarely interact with it directly. PHP runs nearly 70 per cent of all websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is the engine behind WordPress, the software that powers about 40 per cent of all websites such as blogs, small business pages, government portals, online shops and news sites.  WHAT ARE THE RISKS OF THE FLAWS? The two vulnerabilities are rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale, a standard industry scoring system. CERT-EU, the European Union's cybersecurity response team, said that rating signals unauthenticated remote code execution, meaning an attacker can run commands on a vulnerable server, over the internet, with no password or account. A single flaw in PHP opens the same door on millions of servers at once. Whoever exploits the flaw controls the website. GoDaddy, a web hosting provider, said that could mean stolen data, defaced pages or full-system compromise. Cloudflare's chief technology officer said early attacks were emerging.  Most small websites are typically run by owners with no security staff, often on shared hosting where they do not manage the server and may not know who updates PHP. Wordfence, a security plugin for WordPress sites, warned that the usual automatic updates will not apply this fix. CERT-EU's guidance is to take affected sites offline rather than leave them exposed. HOW WAS IT FOUND? Researchers at security firm Calif, working with OpenAI, reported the first flaw to PHP on August 11 after finding it with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, the company said. Wiz, a security firm owned by Alphabet's Google, found the flaws independently and reported a second one on August 24, also using AI models. Wiz said the findings "rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history." The underlying flaws had been present for decades, the firm said, but proving they were exploitable required a chain of steps "at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve." US President Donald Trump's administration said it was "tracking and coordinating with federal agencies and leading SI labs to expedite the release of the fix," referring to Trump's preferred name for artificial intelligence. It framed the discovery as evidence that American "Super Intelligence" strengthens national security.

LONDON/PARIS, Oct 21 : Financial regulators in Europe are questioning Google after a cloud computing outage on Tuesday left millions of bank customers without access to key financial services for hours. The European Banking Authority said that it had been in contact with Google Cloud to obtain further information on the incident, understand its implications and assess its potential impact on financial entities in the EU, a spokesperson for the watchdog told Reuters. Alphabet's Google said the disruption, which lasted several hours, was caused by a "power event" in a London-based network that serves customers across Europe. Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC were among the banks affected. HSBC and Lloyds did not comment.

A Google spokesperson said: "We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis." At Revolut, which has around 13 million UK customers, a wide range of services including logging in, card payments and cash withdrawals were affected on Tuesday, according to the bank's website. Revolut said in a statement that it was reviewing the incident to reduce the impact of any future third-party disruptions, and that customer funds and data had remained safe throughout. The outage is the first major test of new rules across Europe designed to strengthen the resilience of technology providers, including cloud firms, on which the financial sector depends. The European Union last year designated 19 technology firms as critical third-party providers to the financial sector, bringing them under joint direct oversight of three financial regulators — including the EBA — for the first time. Britain took similar steps for four cloud providers, citing the risk that an outage at a major supplier could affect multiple financial firms at the same time. Google Cloud falls under both regulatory frameworks. "The designation of a provider as a Critical third-party provider establishes an EU-level oversight framework; it does not transfer responsibility for incident management from the provider or relieve financial entities of their own regulatory obligations," the EBA said in emailed comments. In Britain, parliament's Treasury Committee has written to the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), seeking details of the regulators' response to the outage on Tuesday, the scale of the disruption and any financial harm caused. The FCA said it was engaging with Google over the incident. Under Britain's critical third party regime, designated providers like Google Cloud must report serious outages to the FCA and the BoE. A spokesperson for the Bank of England declined to comment. Under EU and UK rules, banks are ultimately responsible for the services they provide to customers, including when they rely on third-party providers.

Source: Reuters

Oct 21 : OpenAI said on Wednesday it was expanding advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, bringing the total to 89, as the AI company beefs up its advertising business to boost revenue ahead of a potential initial public offering. The company said in August its ads business had reached an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion. • OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT in the US earlier this year, and more than 100,000 advertisers have since run campaigns on the platform, the company said • The expansion adds 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Peru, following launches in Mexico and Brazil

AMSTERDAM, Oct 21 : Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang believes that Europe's engineering expertise gives it an edge in physical AI and robotics, he said on Wednesday as the US tech giant announced expanded partnerships with European manufacturers and startups. "Every company in Europe will become an AI company," Huang said at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin, which caps a European tour that has already taken him through London, Paris, Stockholm and Dublin. "No region has dedicated itself to making mechatronics, electronics and mechanical systems at the level of precision and craft as the European region." In a demonstration of Europe's AI creativity, Huang shared the stage with tiny duck-shaped, AI-trained robots developed by French startup Pollen Robotics in collaboration with Hugging Face, asking them to perform somersaults.

Nvidia says it has committed nearly $10 billion to Europe's technology ecosystem. It has established an early lead in supplying the processors and software needed for robotic 'brains', giving it a commercial interest in Europe's industry succeeding. Among partnerships announced on Wednesday, Germany's Agile Robots plans to produce 1,000 to 2,000 petite humanoids next year in collaboration with Nvidia, CEO Zhaopeng Chen told Reuters. Production is due to begin late this year. Huang said that Europe — often left behind by the US and Asia in the AI race and with no real home-grown player at the scale of an Nvidia, Anthropic or OpenAI — needed to make sure it was playing a central role. "To be part of this AI economy, you don't want to just be consuming the AI; you want to be producing the AI. We could do all of that here in Europe," he said. Separately on Wednesday, Nvidia showcased a so-called new DSX POD design for factory-built data centre modules using its Vera Rubin platform. It said the modules could be deployed in as little as two weeks, down from six months. However, not all went to plan on stage. The Microducks showed that even with the power of AI, getting robots to follow instructions is not foolproof. Three promptly keeled over when Huang ordered them to take a nap, but the fourth needed extra persuasion.  One appeared distracted and faced the wrong way as Huang wrapped up his speech. "Pay attention, stay focused," he told it sternly.

Source: Reuters
